newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss not compensated with Holocaust funds - report.
newsitem.headline: Swiss not compensated with Holocaust funds - report.

text.p: An official Swiss report on Thursday rejected charges that Swiss citizens were directly paid with money from Holocaust victims to settle claims for communist-seized property in Eastern Europe after World War Two.
Switzerland has struggled to cope with a flood of criticism from world Jewish groups about the way it handled accounts left ownerless by murdered Jews and other victims of Nazi oppression.
"It would be wrong to say this," said historian Peter Hug, one of the authors, when asked by Reuters whether the funds were used to compensate Swiss citizens.

But the government-commissioned report by two independent historians said Berne should consider "concrete compensation measures" for years of mistakes in handling unclaimed bank accounts that may have stemmed from victims of Nazi terror.

It also urged Switzerland to use its comprehensive federal archives to hunt belatedly for East Europeans, including any Holocaust survivors, whose Swiss wealth was declared ownerless after the war and who fell victim to Cold War politics.

The report said Switzerland assigned funds from dormant accounts to communist-ruled Poland and Hungary under postwar compensation accords for confiscated Swiss property, in line with principles of international private law.
The money helped both countries meet compensation payments, but this was not tantamount to paying off Swiss citizens, it said.

Switzerland, pressed by foreign critics, commissioned the report in October to answer accusations by Jewish critics and a U.S. senator that it had used Holocaust victims' riches to compensate Swiss citizens for their seized property.

The report confirmed that Switzerland had paid Poland 16,000 Swiss francs in 1960 from accounts the Poles claimed under international law as reverting to them since the missing owners had last lived in Poland.

Berne in 1975 paid Poland a larger sum of 464,000 francs and Hungary 325,000 francs based on the same home-country claim, but this time paid them from a 1960s fund for bank accounts left ownerless by Jews and other victims of Nazi persecution.

Similar claims from other eastern European countries behind the Iron Curtain were rejected and the report said Poland and Hungary had signed agreements to recognise the claims of rightful heirs if they turned up.
The 1960s fund for ownerless accounts, which totalled about 10 million Swiss francs, was created by a government-ordered sweep of Swiss bank accounts for assets left by Nazi victims.

But the report confirmed that the search for survivors or heirs was restricted to the West by a Swiss policy that barred research behind the Iron Curtain, on the assumption that enquiries could endanger residents of communist countries.

"We recommend that the Swiss Federal Archive's wholly preserved and well-ordered dossiers on East European accounts declared ownerless be reviewed and any surviving contact persons be sought quickly," the report said.
The payment to Hungary was a confidential amendment to a 1973 treaty under which Switzerland deducted Hungary's claims for dormant accounts from Swiss claims for compensation.

"Hungarian counterclaims for a total of 400,000 francs were directly netted off against the sum of 1.8 million francs in compensation owed Swiss property owners," it said, but both governments announced only the net 1.4 million figure.
The historians also said the Swiss government had made repeated mistakes in handling the issue of ownerless accounts, including paying Hungary in secret without notifying parliament.
"Considering the decades of omissions, it is recommended that further steps be considered in order to fulfil today's perception of justice," the report said.
It said those measures would include further research as well as "concrete compensation measures", but did not not specifiy them or say who should be compensated.
Berne is setting up a broad historical enquiry into Switzerland's wartime role as a financial centre. Swiss banks and Jewish groups are also probing the fate of dormant accounts.
